choices.text: A group of atoms within a molecule that has a characteristic chemical behavior
The longest chain of carbon atoms in a molecule
choices.why: The carbon chain's length doesn't set a molecule's chemistry; the groups of atoms with characteristic behavior do.

choices.text: Any atom in a molecule other than carbon and hydrogen
choices.why: Some functional groups, such as alkenes and alkynes, contain only carbon and hydrogen: a C=C or C≡C bond is itself a functional group.

choices.text: A group of atoms whose behavior changes from one molecule to the next
choices.why: The opposite: a given functional group behaves in nearly the same way in every molecule it's a part of.

explanation: Functional groups are the structural features that let compounds be classified into families. A functional group is a group of atoms within a molecule that has a characteristic chemical behavior, and it behaves in nearly the same way in every molecule it's a part of.

prompt: Ethylene is a small plant hormone, and menthene is a much more complicated molecule from peppermint oil. Why do both react with Br2 in the same way?

choices.text: Both contain a carbon–carbon double-bond functional group
Both are natural products made by plants
choices.why: Where a molecule comes from doesn't decide its reactions; the functional group it contains does.

choices.text: Both have the same molecular size
choices.why: Menthene is much larger and more complex. Size and complexity are not important here (Figure 3.1.1).

choices.text: Both contain a carbon–oxygen double bond
choices.why: Neither reaction involves a C=O group. The shared feature is the C=C double bond.

explanation: Both substances contain a carbon–carbon double-bond functional group with a similar polarity pattern, so both react with Br2 in the same way (Figure 3.1.1). The chemistry of every organic molecule, regardless of size and complexity, is determined by the functional groups it contains.

prompt: When ethylene reacts with Br2, a Br atom adds to each of the double-bond carbons. How many Br atoms does the product contain?
explanation: A double bond joins two carbons, and one Br atom adds to each of them, so the product has 2 Br atoms. Menthene reacts the same way at its C=C bond (Figure 3.1.1).

prompt: An arene has alternating double and single bonds in a six-membered ring of carbon atoms. How many carbon–carbon double bonds are drawn in the ring?
explanation: Six ring bonds that alternate double, single, double, single, double, single give 3 double bonds and 3 single bonds.

prompt: Which three functional-group families all contain carbon–carbon multiple bonds?

choices.text: Alkenes, alkynes and arenes
Alkenes, alkynes and nitriles
choices.why: A nitrile's triple bond, –C≡N, is between carbon and nitrogen, not between two carbons.

choices.text: Aldehydes, ketones and esters
choices.why: These contain a carbon–oxygen double bond (a carbonyl group), not a carbon–carbon one.

choices.text: Alkyl halides, alcohols and ethers
choices.why: These have a carbon singly bonded to an electronegative atom.

explanation: Alkenes have a C=C double bond, alkynes a C≡C triple bond, and arenes alternating double and single bonds in a six-membered carbon ring. They look different, but their structural similarities give them chemical similarities.

prompt: CH3OCH3 and CH3OH both contain a carbon singly bonded to oxygen. What makes CH3OCH3 an ether rather than an alcohol?

choices.text: Two carbon atoms are bonded to the same oxygen
Its oxygen carries a hydroxyl group, –OH
choices.why: That describes an alcohol such as CH3OH. CH3OCH3 has no O–H bond.

choices.text: Its oxygen is double-bonded to carbon
choices.why: A C=O double bond is a carbonyl group. Ethers have only single C–O bonds.

choices.text: It contains two oxygen atoms
choices.why: CH3OCH3 has a single oxygen, shared by the two carbons.

explanation: Alcohols have a carbon atom bonded to the oxygen of a hydroxyl group (–OH), while ethers have two carbon atoms bonded to the same oxygen. Table 3.1.1 gives CH3OH (methanol) and CH3OCH3 (dimethyl ether) as examples.

prompt: To which family does CH3SSCH3 belong?

choices.text: Disulfide
Sulfide
choices.why: A sulfide has two carbons bonded to the same sulfur, as in CH3SCH3. Here two sulfurs are joined together.

choices.text: Thiol
choices.why: A thiol has a carbon bonded to the sulfur of an –SH group, as in CH3SH. CH3SSCH3 has no S–H bond.

choices.text: Sulfoxide
choices.why: A sulfoxide has an oxygen on its sulfur. CH3SSCH3 contains no oxygen.

explanation: Disulfides have carbon atoms bonded to two sulfurs that are joined together. Table 3.1.1 gives CH3SSCH3, dimethyl disulfide, as the example, alongside CH3SH (methanethiol) and CH3SCH3 (dimethyl sulfide).

prompt: In alkyl halides, alcohols, amines and thiols, carbon is singly bonded to an electronegative atom. How is the charge distributed in that bond?

choices.text: Carbon bears a partial positive charge (δ+) and the electronegative atom a partial negative charge (δ−)
Carbon bears a partial negative charge (δ−) and the electronegative atom a partial positive charge (δ+)
choices.why: The electronegative atom pulls the bonding electrons toward itself, so it is the one that becomes δ−.

choices.text: The bond is nonpolar, since it is only a single bond
choices.why: Polarity comes from the difference in electronegativity, not the number of bonds. These single bonds are polar.

choices.text: Carbon carries a full positive charge and the other atom a full negative charge
choices.why: These are polar covalent bonds with partial charges (δ+ and δ−), not ionic bonds with full charges.

explanation: In all of these functional groups the bonds are polar, with the carbon atom bearing a partial positive charge (δ+) and the electronegative atom (halogen, oxygen, nitrogen or sulfur) bearing a partial negative charge (δ−).

prompt: What feature defines an organophosphate such as methyl phosphate, CH3OPO3^2−?

choices.text: A carbon atom bonded to the oxygen of a phosphate group
A carbon atom bonded directly to phosphorus
choices.why: In methyl phosphate the carbon is attached to an oxygen, and that oxygen is attached to the phosphorus: CH3–O–PO3^2−.

choices.text: A carbon–oxygen double bond
choices.why: That is a carbonyl group. Organophosphates have a carbon singly bonded to an oxygen.

choices.text: Two phosphorus atoms joined through oxygen
choices.why: That describes a diphosphate, such as methyl diphosphate, CH3OP2O6^3−. A monophosphate has one phosphorus.

explanation: Organophosphates have a carbon atom bonded to the oxygen of a phosphate group (–OPO3^2−). Table 3.1.1 gives methyl phosphate, CH3OPO3^2−, and methyl diphosphate, CH3OP2O6^3−, as examples.

prompt: In aldehydes, ketones, amides and the other carbonyl-containing groups, how is the C=O bond polarized?

choices.text: The carbonyl carbon is δ+ and the oxygen is δ−
The carbonyl carbon is δ− and the oxygen is δ+
choices.why: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it draws electron density toward itself and becomes δ−.

choices.text: The C=O bond is nonpolar because it is a double bond
choices.why: A double bond between atoms of different electronegativity is still polar.

choices.text: The polarity depends on which group is attached, so it is reversed in amides
choices.why: In all of the carbonyl functional groups the carbon is δ+ and the oxygen δ−.

explanation: In all of the functional groups that contain a carbonyl group, C=O, the carbonyl carbon atom bears a partial positive charge (δ+) and the oxygen atom bears a partial negative charge (δ−).

prompt: How does an aldehyde differ from a ketone?

choices.text: An aldehyde has at least one H atom bonded to the C=O; a ketone has two carbon atoms bonded to it
An aldehyde has an –OH group bonded to the C=O; a ketone has two carbons
choices.why: An –OH bonded to the C=O makes a carboxylic acid, not an aldehyde.

choices.text: An aldehyde has a C–O single bond; a ketone has a C=O double bond
choices.why: Both contain the carbonyl group, C=O. They differ in what is attached to the carbonyl carbon.

choices.text: An aldehyde has two carbons bonded to the C=O; a ketone has at least one H
choices.why: This is reversed. Ketones, such as propanone, have a carbon on each side of the C=O.

explanation: Aldehydes have at least one H atom bonded to the C=O, and ketones have two carbon atoms bonded to the C=O. Their names end in -al and -one (Table 3.1.1).

prompt: Both amines and amides contain nitrogen. What distinguishes an amide?

choices.text: Its nitrogen is bonded to a C=O carbon
Its nitrogen is bonded to a carbon by a single bond, with no carbonyl group
choices.why: That describes an amine, such as methylamine, CH3NH2.

choices.text: Its nitrogen is triple-bonded to carbon
choices.why: A C≡N triple bond is a nitrile, such as ethanenitrile.

choices.text: Its nitrogen carries a lone pair, which amines lack
choices.why: Table 3.1.1 shows a lone pair on nitrogen in both amines and amides. The difference is the C=O bonded to the amide nitrogen.

explanation: Amines have a carbon atom bonded to a nitrogen, while amides have an amine-like nitrogen bonded to the C=O. Amide names end in -amide (Table 3.1.1).

prompt: What is bonded to the C=O in a thioester?

choices.text: A sulfide-like sulfur
An –SH group, with no carbonyl present
choices.why: An –SH group on a carbon with no C=O is a thiol.

choices.text: A chlorine atom
choices.why: A chlorine bonded to the C=O makes an acid chloride.

choices.text: An –OH group
choices.why: An –OH bonded to the C=O makes a carboxylic acid.

explanation: Thioesters have a sulfide-like sulfur bonded to the C=O. Their names end in -thioate, as in methyl ethanethioate (Table 3.1.1).

prompt: Ethanoyl chloride and chloromethane, CH3Cl, both contain chlorine. Why is ethanoyl chloride an acid chloride and not an alkyl halide?

choices.text: Its chlorine is bonded to the carbon of a C=O group
It contains more than one chlorine atom
choices.why: The number of chlorines doesn't decide the family. An acid chloride has a chlorine bonded to the C=O.

choices.text: Its chlorine is bonded to oxygen
choices.why: In an acid chloride the chlorine is bonded to the carbonyl carbon, not to the oxygen.

choices.text: Its carbon–chlorine bond is not polar
choices.why: Carbon–chlorine bonds are polar in both. The difference is that the acid chloride's carbon is also double-bonded to oxygen.

explanation: Alkyl halides have a carbon atom bonded to a halogen (–X), as in chloromethane, CH3Cl. Acid chlorides have a chlorine bonded to the C=O, and their names end in -oyl chloride (Table 3.1.1).

prompt: Which of these functional groups does NOT contain a carbonyl group?

choices.text: Ether
Ester
choices.why: Esters contain a C=O; their names end in -oate, as in methyl ethanoate.

choices.text: Amide
choices.why: An amide has an amine-like nitrogen bonded to a C=O.

choices.text: Ketone
choices.why: A ketone has two carbon atoms bonded to a C=O.

explanation: An ether has two carbons singly bonded to the same oxygen, with no C=O. Esters, amides and ketones are among the functional groups with a carbon–oxygen double bond (carbonyl group).

prompt: According to Table 3.1.1, a compound whose name ends in -one, such as propanone, belongs to which family?

choices.text: Ketone
Aldehyde
choices.why: Aldehyde names end in -al, as in ethanal.

choices.text: Alcohol
choices.why: Alcohol names end in -ol, as in methanol.

choices.text: Alkene
choices.why: Alkene names end in -ene, as in ethene.

explanation: Table 3.1.1 lists the name ending -one for ketones (example: propanone), -al for aldehydes, -ol for alcohols and -ene for alkenes.

prompt: According to Table 3.1.1, the name methyl ethanoate ends in -oate. Which functional group does that ending indicate?

choices.text: Ester
Carboxylic acid
choices.why: Carboxylic acid names end in -oic acid, as in ethanoic acid.

choices.text: Thioester
choices.why: Thioester names end in -thioate, as in methyl ethanethioate.

choices.text: Carboxylic acid anhydride
choices.why: Anhydride names end in -oic anhydride, as in ethanoic anhydride.

explanation: Table 3.1.1 gives the ending -oate for esters (methyl ethanoate), -oic acid for carboxylic acids, -thioate for thioesters and -oic anhydride for carboxylic acid anhydrides.

prompt: Which functional group has no characteristic name ending in Table 3.1.1?

choices.text: Halide
Alcohol
choices.why: Alcohols end in -ol, as in methanol.

choices.text: Amine
choices.why: Amines end in -amine, as in methylamine.

choices.text: Nitrile
choices.why: Nitriles end in -nitrile, as in ethanenitrile.

explanation: Table 3.1.1 lists "None" as the name ending for halides (example: chloromethane, CH3Cl), as well as for arenes and imines. Alcohols end in -ol, amines in -amine and nitriles in -nitrile.
